title: Cold Soak or Straight to Heat
summary: A cold overnight soak pulls a great deal of colour out before any heat is applied, which means the pot needs less time hot and is far less likely to brown. Straight to heat is faster and shallower. For anything you care about, soak first.
body: Two ways to start a bark bath, and the difference shows up in the finished colour rather than in the pot.
## The two starts

| Aspect | Cold soak, then heat | Straight to heat |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time before fibre enters | 8 to 24 hours, then 1 hour hot | About 1 hour |
| Time at temperature | Short | Long |
| Browning risk | Low | Higher |
| Depth | Fuller | Adequate |
| Best for | Anything you care about | A test pot, a rush job |

The reason the cold soak wins is simple. Water moves colour out of bark without help; heat only speeds it up. A bath that soaked overnight is already loaded when you light the stove, so it needs far less time hot — and time hot is what turns purple into brown.
## How to run a cold soak

1. Weigh the bark against your dry fibre weight. See [how much bark per pound of fibre](/blog/weighing-bark-against-fibre).
2. Put it in a mesh bag in the pot and cover it with cool water.
3. Leave it 8 to 24 hours, somewhere cool. Overnight is the usual.
4. Bring it up slowly to about 80°C / 175°F and hold for an hour.
5. Lift the bag out and strain what needs straining.
6. Enter the wet, mordanted fibre.
## Solar and long cold baths

In summer a jar on a sunny windowsill for a week will dye wool without ever reaching a simmer, and the purples from a long cold bath are often the cleanest you will get from this material. It is slow and it is unpredictable about depth, and for some work it is exactly right.
Do not leave a cold bath standing warm for a week in a closed room, though. It ferments, it smells, and a sour bath dyes unevenly.
## Which cut suits which

Powder loads a cold soak quickly because of its surface area, so an overnight soak with powder is nearly as strong as a hot bath. Shredded and stripped bark benefit more from the long soak, because water needs time to reach the inside of a piece.
## What this material is not

Everything described here is raw botanical material sold for dyeing, soap making and craft work. It is not food, it is not a supplement, and it is not for human consumption. Nothing on this page is a recommendation to put any of it in or on a body.

title: Eight Faults That Spoil a First Bath
summary: Almost every disappointing first bath comes down to eight things: boiling it, skipping the scour, undissolved alum, weighing wet fibre, leaving material loose in the pot, packing the pot, judging colour wet, and changing three variables at once. None is expensive to fix.
body: We hear about the same eight faults over and over, which is good news: they are all cheap to correct, and none of them is the material's doing.
## 1. Boiling it

The single commonest fault and the only one that cannot be undone. A rolling boil takes this colour to brown in minutes. Work at about 80°C / 175°F — small bubbles on the base of the pot, nothing breaking the surface. Buy a thermometer before you buy more bark. See [keeping a bark bath purple](/blog/keeping-a-bark-bath-purple).
## 2. Not scouring
Spinning oil, lanolin and factory sizing all repel water, and fibre that wets unevenly dyes unevenly. A hot wash with a pH-neutral detergent before mordanting is not optional.
## 3. Undissolved alum

A crystal that has not dissolved mordants the spot it settles against far more heavily than the rest, and the bath afterwards shows it as a hard-edged pale patch. Dissolve alum in a jug of very hot water before it goes in the pot. See [mordanting wool before a bark bath](/blog/mordanting-wool-before-a-bark-bath).
## 4. Weighing wet fibre
Every ratio in dyeing is a percentage of dry fibre weight. Wet wool holds several times its weight in water, so a damp weighing makes both the alum and the bark quantities wrong.
## 5. Loose material against the fibre

Bark and especially powder pressed against wool leaves specks that do not rinse out of the plies. Use a mesh bag, or strain before the fibre enters. See [filtering a bark bath](/blog/filtering-a-bark-bath-without-losing-the-colour).
## 6. Packing the pot

Fibre crammed into too little water dyes pale where it touched itself. Use enough water that a skein can be lifted and turned without force. Volume does not dilute the colour — depth comes from the ratio, not the concentration.
## 7. Judging the colour wet
Wet fibre reads one to two shades darker than it will dry. Squeeze a strand, dry it against a warm mug, and judge that. Pulling a skein too early is the second commonest regret after boiling.
## 8. Changing three things at once
A bath where temperature, ratio and pH all moved teaches nothing, because nothing can be attributed. Change one variable per pot and write down what you did. The notebook is the actual skill.
## The cheap way to learn all eight

Test pots. A fistful of bark, a small jar and a metre of the same yarn costs almost nothing and answers the question before a fleece is at risk. See [testing a dye before you commit a fleece](/blog/testing-a-dye-before-you-commit-a-fleece).

title: Does the Colour Last? Testing Light and Washing at Home
summary: Two tests answer it. Tape half a dyed sample in a south-facing window for four weeks and compare the halves for light fastness; wash another sample four times with a white swatch alongside for wash fastness. Both cost nothing and take one evening to set up.
body: Fastness is two separate properties, and a dye can be good at one and poor at the other. Anyone selling or gifting dyed work should know which they have.
## Light fastness, the window test

1. Dye a strip of the fibre, or use a length of the finished yarn.
2. Cut it in two. Put one half in a drawer.
3. Tape the other to the inside of a south-facing window, with card covering its left half.
4. Leave it four to eight weeks. Longer is better.
5. Compare all three: the drawer piece, the covered half, the exposed half.
The card is what makes it a test rather than an impression, because a fade you can only see against the original is the fade a customer will notice in a year.
## Wash fastness, the multi-wash test

Wash a dyed sample four times in warm water with a pH-neutral detergent, with a white swatch of the same fibre pinned to it. Then look at two things: whether the sample lost depth, and whether the white swatch picked colour up. The second matters more — a dye that bleeds will bleed onto everything else in the machine.

| What you see | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Sample holds, swatch stays white | Well mordanted, properly rinsed |
| Sample holds, swatch tints | Unfixed surplus left in the fibre; wash again before use |
| Sample loses depth in wash one, then holds | Normal — that was the surplus coming off |
| Sample keeps losing depth | Mordant step failed |
## What to expect from a tannin bark on wool

Properly mordanted, wool and silk hold this colour well in washing. Light is the harder test: like most plant colours it softens in strong sun, moving towards a warmer, browner tone rather than simply going pale. That is a reason to be honest about it, not a reason to avoid it — keep dyed pieces out of permanent direct sun and they hold for years.
Iron-modified shades generally hold their depth better in light than the unmodified purple. See [iron as a modifier](/blog/iron-as-a-modifier-how-far-to-go).
## Two habits that improve both results
**Rinse until the water runs clear**, and wash once with detergent before the piece goes into use. Most apparent bleeding is surplus colour that was never bonded.
**Do not overload the bath.** Fibre cannot hold more than it can hold; the surplus sits on the surface and comes off in the first wash, taking your confidence with it.

title: Bark as a Colourant in Cold Process Soap
summary: Soap is alkaline, and alkali pushes a tannin colour towards tan, khaki and brown rather than the purple it gives on wool. Use one to two teaspoons of finely milled powder per pound of oils, added at a light trace, and expect the shade to keep shifting for a fortnight.
body: Botanical colourants behave differently in soap than in a dye pot, and this one changes more than most. The reason is pH: fresh soap batter sits around pH 10 or higher, and tannins read alkali as a colour instruction.
## What colour to expect

Not purple. On wool at neutral pH this bark gives aubergine and maroon; in soap batter it lands in tan, dusty rose-brown, khaki or greyish beige depending on your oils and how much you use. A batch that looks promisingly pink at the mould often settles to putty a week later.
Plan for brown tones and you will like the result. Plan for purple and you will not.
## Quantities

| Powder per pound of oils | Result |
| --- | --- |
| ½ tsp | A faint warm tint |
| 1 to 2 tsp | The usual range — tan to soft brown |
| 1 tbsp and above | Deep brown, and noticeable scratch in the bar |
Only finely milled powder is worth using. Shredded or stripped bark gives specks and a rough bar; if that is the look you want, use it deliberately and say so.
## Method

1. **Disperse it first.** A teaspoon of powder into a tablespoon of your warmed oils, stirred smooth, then set aside. Powder added dry to batter clumps and never recovers.
2. **Add at a light trace**, not before. Colourant in the lye water takes the worst of the alkali and usually goes muddier.
3. **Blend briefly** — just enough to be even.
4. **Expect acceleration.** Tannins can thicken batter faster than you expect, so keep intricate swirls for a recipe you know.
5. **Judge it at two weeks**, not at cutting. The shade moves as the bar rests and hardens.
## Two practical warnings
**It stains moulds and towels.** Silicone comes clean; wooden moulds and pale cloth keep a memory.
**Test a small batch first.** A one-pound test batch answers the colour question for the cost of a bar, and soap makers who skip it tend to lose a full loaf to a shade they did not want.
## Why buying by the pound makes sense here

Soap colourant uses teaspoons per batch, so a pound of powder goes a very long way, and working from one batch keeps your bars consistent across a run. Different batches of bark differ in tone, which is invisible in a dye pot and obvious on a shelf of soap.

title: A Plain Glossary of Natural Dyeing Terms
summary: The vocabulary is small and most of it is old. Mordant, scour, WOF, exhaust bath, modifier, fastness, protein and cellulose fibre, tannin, substantive and adjective dyes — twenty terms cover nearly every instruction you will read, and knowing them makes older books usable.
body: Natural dyeing instructions are often written in terms nobody defines, because the books assume a teacher. Here they are in plain language.
## The core terms

| Term | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Mordant** | A mineral salt, usually alum, that bonds fibre and colour so it stays. From the Latin for "to bite". |
| **Scour** | Washing fibre before mordanting, to remove grease, oil and sizing. |
| **WOF** | Weight of fibre — the dry weight everything else is a percentage of. |
| **Dye bath** | The liquid holding the colour, with the plant material strained out or bagged. |
| **Exhaust bath** | The second or third bath from material already used once. Lighter each time. |
| **Modifier** | Something added after dyeing to shift the shade: iron, an alkali, an acid. |
| **Fastness** | How well colour survives light and washing. Two separate properties. |
## Fibre words

| Term | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Protein fibre** | From animals: wool, silk, alpaca, mohair. Takes this colour deeply. |
| **Cellulose fibre** | From plants: cotton, linen, hemp. Needs a tannin step as well as alum. |
| **Skein** | A loosely wound loop of yarn, tied in several places so it cannot tangle in the pot. |
| **Felting** | Wool fibres locking together permanently from heat plus agitation. Not reversible. |
| **Handle** | How a fibre feels. Too much mordant ruins it; people notice before they can name it. |
## Colour words

| Term | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Tannin** | A group of plant compounds that bind protein and give colour. This bark is rich in them. See [what tannins do in a dye bath](/blog/what-tannins-do-in-a-dye-bath). |
| **Substantive dye** | A colour that holds without a mordant. Tannin-rich material is partly substantive. |
| **Adjective dye** | A colour that needs a mordant. Most plant colours. |
| **Overdyeing** | Dyeing an already-dyed fibre a second colour to build a third. |
| **Shifted** | A shade moved by pH or a modifier rather than by the dye itself. |
| **Strike** | How fast a colour takes hold. Fast strike gives blotches; slow strike gives even colour. |
## Material words

| Term | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Cut** | The physical form: powder, shredded, or stripped lengths. |
| **Powder** | Milled fine. Fast, strong, needs straining. |
| **Shredded** | Coarse pieces. Slower, easy to strain, re-baths well. |
| **Stripped** | Whole inner-bark lengths, closest to how it came off the root. |
## Reading old instructions

Two habits make older books usable. First, read every quantity as a percentage of dry fibre weight even when the book gives handfuls. Second, ignore any instruction to boil: older texts say boil freely because they were written for madder and onion skins, and a tannin bark browns where those do not.
